# Mahāli Sutta (DN 6 (PTS DN i 150))

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Mahāli Sutta* is the sixth discourse of the *Dīghanikāya*, set at the Gabled Hall (Kūṭāgārasālā) in Vesālī [Buswell & Lopez 2014]. The narrative begins when the Buddha's attendant Nāgita informs a delegation of visiting brāhmaṇas that the Buddha is in seclusion [Freedman 1977]. The Licchavi leader Mahāli approaches the Buddha regarding the former monk Sunakkhatta, who claimed to perceive divine forms but could not hear heavenly sounds; the Buddha explains that such meditative attainments correspond strictly to the manner in which meditation is cultivated [Buswell & Lopez 2014]. He clarifies that disciples do not embrace the monastic holy life to obtain supernormal vision or hearing, but rather to abandon the fetters and attain the four successive stages of awakening—from stream-entry to arahantship—via the noble eightfold path [Norman 1983; Prebish; Buswell & Lopez 2014; Wen].

Scholars have noted that the sutta consists of two distinct parts [Norman 1983]. The second section incorporates the question posed by the mendicant Jāliya on whether the soul or life-principle (*jīva*) is identical to or distinct from the body [Gyatso 1992; Norman 1983; Buswell & Lopez 2014]. This question is answered through a recapitulation of the gradual training and the attainment of arahantship as expounded in the *Sāmaññaphala Sutta* (DN 2) [Kingsbury 2002; Norman 1983; Buswell & Lopez 2014]. K. R. Norman suggests that the Jāliya material was incorporated into the *Mahālisutta* at an early date before the compilation of the modern *Dīghanikāya*, noting that ethical conduct (*sīla*) is mentioned only in the Jāliya portion, without which the text would lack grounds for inclusion in the *Sīlakkhandhavagga* [Kingsbury 2002; Norman 1983]. Oskar von Hinüber suggests that textual variations across DN 6, 7, 10, and 12 arose from different geographical centers among the Dīghabhāṇakas [Kingsbury 2002].

The *Mahāli Sutta* has no direct counterpart in the Chinese *Dīrghāgama* or other Chinese Āgama collections [Banerjee 1979; Kingsbury 2002; Buswell & Lopez 2014]. Extant external witnesses are limited to Sanskrit manuscript fragments (SHT sutta 19). Internally, it largely duplicates the subsequent *Jāliya Sutta* (DN 7); DharmaNexus registers massive text reuse between the two, notably an alignment of over 17,000 characters spanning DN 6 §15.2–19.11 and DN 7 §1.3–5.11 [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus also records shared stock passages with the *Saḷāyatana Saṁyutta* (SN 35) and cross-language alignments with the Chinese *Madhyamāgama* (T 26) and the Sanskrit *Arthaviniścayasūtra* [DharmaNexus]. Canonical and post-canonical Theravāda treatises cite the sutta, including the *Mahāniddesa* (Mnd 14) and the *Kathāvatthu* (Kv 10.3, 18.9).
